R0081.title: Supply Chain Risk
R0081.definition: Supply chain risk refers to the possibility that products such as software, hardware, and cloud services are exposed to security threats during development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance due to potential threats in supply chain components or links.
R0081.description:
Supply chain risk spans the development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance of software, hardware, cloud services, and outsourced operations. Attackers may abuse upstream components, build environments, vendor accounts, or delivery processes to introduce malicious code, backdoor settings, or vulnerable components.

This risk rarely stays within a single system. It can propagate through dependency chains and downstream customers, so organizations need supplier governance, component provenance, build integrity, release signing, runtime monitoring, and emergency replacement plans.
R0081.influence: Supply-chain risk can propagate weaknesses in upstream components, build environments, delivery processes, or supplier accounts into many downstream systems, causing malicious-code implantation, persistent backdoors, sensitive data exposure, and business disruption. Because affected organizations usually trust suppliers and delivered artifacts, discovery is often delayed and response may require emergency component replacement, version rollback, service suspension, or a full supplier-security review.

references.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations
ENISA Threat Landscape for Supply Chain Attacks

observables: Upstream components or dependencies show anomalous version updates, and build-artifact hashes do not match the official ones
Vendor accounts show anomalous logins or are hijacked and then used to submit suspicious code
Delivery signatures fail verification or the build environment is found tampered with
Newly introduced components have unknown provenance, and SCA scans flag known-malicious packages or suspicious licenses

R0081-001.title: Software Supply Chain Risk
R0081-001.definition: Software supply chain risk refers to the possibility that software systems are exposed to security threats during development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance due to potential threats in supply chain components or links.
R0081-001.description: Scenarios include third-party components being attacked, suppliers suffering data breaches, and software development tools being tampered with, potentially leading to malicious code injection, backdoors, or data leakage.
R0081-001.influence: Software supply-chain poisoning can introduce malicious dependencies, backdoor code, or tampered build artifacts into many downstream applications, causing credential exposure, remote control of business systems, customer data exfiltration, and service disruption. Because these issues often appear as normal version updates or trusted components, investigation and rollback are costly, and affected organizations must re-audit dependency sources, build pipelines, and release signatures.

references.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1
CISA: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities

observables: Third-party component or dependency updates introduce anomalous code or backdoors, and the new version does not match official release notes
Software development tools or CI environments are tampered with, with anomalous build-artifact hashes
Vendor source-code repositories show anomalous commits or permission changes
SCA scans of downstream applications flag suspicious dependencies or known-malicious packages

R0081-002.title: Hardware Supply Chain Risk
R0081-002.definition: Hardware supply chain risk refers to the possibility that hardware systems are exposed to security threats during development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance due to potential threats in supply chain components or links.
R0081-002.description:
Hardware supply chain risk spans chips, motherboards, firmware, system assembly, logistics, refurbishment, deployment, and maintenance. Attackers, malicious suppliers, or compromised intermediaries may replace components, modify BIOS, UEFI, or device firmware, preload malware, or implant keyloggers, radio transmitters, and hardware network pivots so that a device arrives with covert access capability already present.

These implants often sit below the operating system and conventional endpoint security, may survive operating-system reinstallation or disk replacement, and can remain hidden behind legitimate device appearance and supply-chain trust. Governance requires supplier qualification, tamper-evident shipping and custody, bill-of-materials and firmware provenance, signature validation, incoming inspection, firmware-integrity monitoring, and investigation of anomalous radio and outbound-network activity.
R0081-002.influence: Hardware supply-chain implants can place firmware backdoors, hardware trojans, or covert eavesdropping modules into devices before delivery, giving attackers low-level persistent control. Such threats may survive operating-system reinstallation or disk replacement, enabling long-term data exfiltration, credential theft, remote takeover of critical devices, and hard-to-trace outages or physical safety incidents in core infrastructure.

references.title: ICT Supply Chain Risk Management Task Force Threat Scenarios Report - CISA
Learning from the Enemy: The GUNMAN Project - GovInfo

observables: Firmware or BIOS hashes of newly purchased hardware do not match the vendor's official signatures
Devices are implanted with backdoors at the factory or during transit, and show anomalous outbound connections at runtime
After a hardware supplier suffers an attack, signs of tampering appear in its device-delivery chain
Chip or firmware layer exhibits anomalous behavior that cannot be detected by conventional software-detection methods

R0081-003.title: Cloud Service Supply Chain Risk
R0081-003.definition: Cloud service supply chain risk refers to the possibility that cloud services are exposed to security threats during development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance due to potential threats in supply chain components or links.
R0081-003.description: Scenarios include third-party components being attacked, suppliers suffering data breaches, and cloud service development tools being tampered with, potentially leading to malicious code injection, backdoors, or data leakage.
R0081-003.influence: Harms include potential business disruption, sensitive information exposure, and system vulnerability exposure, significantly impacting the organization's trust and reliability.

references.title: NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 Update 1: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations

observables: A security incident at a cloud provider exposes tenant data or causes service disruption
A third-party component of the cloud service is tampered with, affecting downstream tenants' runtime environments
Cloud-provider accounts are hijacked and used to anomalously operate tenant resources
The cloud platform's development toolchain is implanted with malicious code, affecting a large number of tenants

R0081-004.title: Outsourced Personnel Risk
R0081-004.definition: Outsourced personnel risk refers to the possibility that software systems are exposed to security threats due to potential threats from the behavior of outsourced personnel involved in software development, delivery, deployment, and maintenance.
R0081-004.description: Scenarios include outsourced personnel's accounts being compromised, maliciously tampered with, or misused, potentially leading to malicious code injection, backdoors, or data leakage.
R0081-004.influence: Harms include potential business disruption, sensitive information exposure, and system vulnerability exposure, significantly impacting the organization's trust and reliability.

observables: Outsourced or on-site personnel accounts log in anomalously, with source IPs or devices inconsistent with prior profiles
Outsourced accounts access core systems or code repositories beyond their authorized duties
Compromised outsourced-personnel accounts submit suspicious code or exfiltrate sensitive data
Outsourced personnel permissions are not revoked promptly after project completion, leaving dormant accounts

R0081-005.title: Open Source Component Poisoning Risk
R0081-005.definition: Attackers publish packages containing malicious code on open source package management platforms (such as npm, PyPI, Maven, etc.) or hijack existing popular open source projects to conduct supply chain attacks against downstream users.
R0081-005.description: Open source component poisoning is a rapidly growing supply chain attack method. Main techniques include: (1) Typosquatting: publishing malicious packages with names similar to popular packages to exploit developer typos. (2) Dependency confusion: exploiting package managers' preference for public repositories to publish malicious public packages with the same name as internal enterprise packages. (3) Maintainer account hijacking: obtaining popular open source project maintainer account access through social engineering or credential leakage to plant malicious code in normal updates. (4) Malicious PR merging: submitting pull requests containing hidden malicious code to popular open source projects. (5) Abandoned package takeover: taking over popular packages abandoned by their original authors and planting malicious code in new versions.
R0081-005.influence: Large numbers of downstream projects are implanted with malicious code, sensitive data is leaked, systems are compromised, and the supply chain trust ecosystem is damaged.

references.title: SLSA: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts

observables: Newly published packages on package managers have names highly similar to popular packages (typosquatting)
Dependency-pull logs show public packages with the same name as internal private packages (dependency confusion)
Maintainer accounts of popular open-source projects make anomalous commits with suspicious updates
SCA scans flag known-malicious packages, or install scripts contain suspicious network callbacks
